title: VC0-02608
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of India, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of India, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant is an orthodox Sikh man from the Punjab. He alleges that he is a member of the Shiromani Akali Dal Amritsar (SAD(A)) political party and that he faces persecution at the hands of supporters of the Dera Sacha Souda (DSS) religious organization.

The RPD dismissed the Appellant's refugee claim because it found that he had embellished certain aspects of his claim and found he had a viable IFA in Delhi. On appeal, the Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of his credibility and in its finding that he has a viable IFA in Delhi. The Appellant did not submit any new evidence on appeal and did not request an oral hearing.
Having conducted an independent assessment of the evidence before me, I find that the RPD was correct in its credibility findings and its conclusion that there is a viable IFA in Delhi.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2 Credibility

I accept that the Appellant is an orthodox Sikh and member of SAD(A). I accept that he fears harm at the hands of DSS supporters, who hold opposing religious and political views. I accept, as the RPD did, that the Appellant faced verbal threats from DSS supporters in 2011 because of the work he was doing at the time to help organize a SAD(A) rally.

The RPD found, however, that the Appellant had embellished certain facts regarding attacks by DSS supporters and the prominence of his role with SAD(A). On appeal, the Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of the evidence regarding attacks by DSS supporters but did not raise any specific arguments regarding the RPD's findings that the Appellant was not a high profile or influential member of SAD(A). I find that the RPD was correct in its factual determinations that the Appellant was not physically harmed by DSS supporters and was not a high profile or influential member of SAD(A). Attacks by Dera Sacha Souda

The Appellant's evidence was inconsistent as to whether he had been physically harmed by DSS supporters. The RPD noted that when interviewed by Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officers, the Appellant stated that he was subjected to verbal threats from DSS supporters but that he was not physically harmed.3 He specified that supporters surrounded him to intimidate him and that he managed to escape. He stated that nothing happened to him in 2012 because he went underground and that there were no other incidents. He stated that he came to Canada in 2013.

In contrast, the Appellant stated in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form narrative that in XXXX 2011 while preparing for a rally, he and other SAD(A) supporters were attacked by a pack of about a hundred men and that he was punched, kicked and beaten with hockey sticks.4 He stated that he received a threatening phone call from a DSS worker after the rally and that a few months later, while visiting family in Moga, he was attacked by five people and was beaten badly with sticks and kicks. He stated he was attacked again on XXXX XXXX, 2012 and was badly beaten and suffered bruises all over his body and had lacerations on his XXXX XXXX and XXXX. He stated that he attended a hospital for treatment and reported the incident to police, but that the police refused to take the report and threatened him instead. He stated his father later learned that the Appellant was on a DSS hit list.

At the RPD hearing on January 13, 2020, the Appellant reiterated that he was attacked three times by DSS supporters.5 When asked by the RPD to explain the discrepancy between the information he provided in his interview with the CBSA and the information in his BOC form and testimony, the Appellant stated that on the day of the CBSA interview he was very sick, very upset, very nervous and very afraid.6 He explained that he was afraid he was going to be sent back to India and was so afraid that he could not say anything. He stated that he could not understand anything and that he did not know whether his case was going to go ahead.

The RPD did not accept the Appellant's explanation for the discrepancy as reasonable. The RPD noted that the interview took place with the assistance of an interpreter and in the presence of the Appellant's counsel. It also noted that the Appellant had previous experience in extending his visa, so he was not completely new to dealing with officials in Canada. It noted that the difference in evidence was significant and involved specific contradictions regarding the nature and frequency of attacks by DSS supporters, which goes to the heart of his refugee claim. Finally, the RPD found that if the Appellant was worried about whether his claim would go ahead, it was reasonable to expect that he would have disclosed to the CBSA more information about the harm he faced, not less.

On appeal, the Appellant raises arguments regarding the credibility and trustworthiness of the CBSA officers' declarations regarding the interviews held with the Appellant. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by referring to two interviews with the CBSA rather than focussing on the one interview where the issue of attacks against him was raised. The Appellant argues that the solemn declaration of the officer who conducted the Minister's Delegate interview7 is not a statutory declaration as defined in the Canada Evidence Act8 and thus has limited evidentiary value. He notes that the declaration is dated March 2, 2020, whereas it is stated at the outset of the declaration that the interview occurred on March 29, 2020. The Appellant submits that the contradictory dates suggest that the declaration contains a fusion of information from two different statements and that it cannot be determined which parts of the declaration pertain to the Appellant. The Appellant argues that there is no explicit admission by him that the salient exchanges recorded by the Minister's Delegate actually took place as none of the exchanges were read to him at the RPD hearing. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in not addressing the Appellant's explanation that he was very sick at the time of the CBSA interview.

I do not accept the Appellant's arguments. I find that the declaration of the Minister's Delegate is a credible and trustworthy account of the interview that occurred on March 29, 2020. Neither the RPD nor the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is bound by any legal or technical rules of evidence9 and both may receive and base a decision on evidence that is adduced in the proceedings and considered credible or trustworthy in the circumstances.10 The CBSA declarations do not need to meet the requirements of a statutory declaration under the Canada Evidence Act to be considered as evidence before the RPD or RAD. However, I do note that, in both declarations, the officers conclude their declarations by stating that they make the solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath. While the declaration of the Minister's Delegate is dated March 2, 2020, I find that this is likely a typographical error and give more weight to the statement earlier in the declaration that the interview occurred on March 29, 2020.

I note that the Appellant was represented by the same counsel at the CBSA Minister's Delegate proceeding, the RPD hearing, and this appeal. At the RPD hearing, the Member asked Counsel to put the CBSA solemn declarations before the Appellant and asked the Appellant a number of questions relating to the CBSA interview where the Appellant made statements regarding the basis for his refugee claim. Counsel did not raise any issue at the RPD hearing regarding the credibility or trustworthiness of the CBSA officer's declaration. Despite asking other follow-up questions to the Appellant during the hearing, Counsel did not ask any questions about the statements made at the CBSA interview or about the credibility and trustworthiness of the officer's declaration regarding the interview.

Similarly, before the RPD, Counsel did not ask any questions to the Appellant and did not make any submissions about the Appellant's testimony that he was very sick at the CBSA interview. In oral submissions, Counsel stated that his client "testified that he was very nervous and very scared during the interviews with CBSA" and does not elaborate on the testimony that the Appellant was very sick.11 On appeal, the Appellant has not submitted any new evidence regarding a medical condition or ailment at the time of the CBSA interview.

Finally, in submissions before the RPD, Counsel conceded that the Appellant "made contradictory statements that do not clearly jibe [sic] with the statement in his Basis of Claim form" and that after repeated questions of why there was a contradiction, the Appellant "maintained that he was really scared and did not know what he was saying."12 Counsel submitted that he would leave it up to the RPD Member as to the weight to give to the contradictions compared to his testimony.

In reviewing the findings of the RPD and in reaching my own findings relating to credibility, I am mindful that there is a presumption of truthfulness when a claimant has sworn to the truth of their allegations unless there are valid reasons to doubt their truthfulness.13 I find that it was correct for the RPD to draw a negative interference regarding the Appellant's credibility given the blatant contradiction in statements from the Appellant regarding the number and severity of his encounters with DSS supporters and the lack of a reasonable explanation. It was correct for the RPD to conclude that the Appellant had not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he had ever been physically harmed by DSS supporters.

The Appellant's explanation that he was sick, nervous, scared and upset during the CBSA interview does not reasonably explain why he would state that he only suffered verbal threats in 2011 and not the three physical assaults in 2011 and 2012 that he mentioned in his BOC form and testimony, particularly when he was asked specifically by the officer if he was ever physically harmed and if he had any problems in 2012.14 While the circumstances of the CBSA interview may have been upsetting to the Appellant and differed from previous experiences with immigration officials as he was detained at the time of the CBSA interview, he was accompanied by counsel at the interview and had the benefit of an interpreter. Given that the Appellant was making a refugee claim and was asked specific questions by an immigration official about whether he was ever physically harmed by the alleged agent of persecution, it is reasonable to expect that the Appellant would have mentioned at this interview that he had been beaten severely on three occasions. The omission of this evidence at the CBSA interview, contradictory statements in response to specific questions, and lack of reasonable explanation for the omission and contradictions leads me to disbelieve that the Appellant was physically harmed on three occasions in India in 2011 and 2012.

The RPD was correct to find that the supporting evidence including the hospital report and affidavits from the Appellant's father and neighbour do not overcome the issues in the credibility of his own statements in order to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he was physically attacked. On appeal, the Appellant does not raise an issue regarding the RPD's assessment of the supporting documents. In reviewing the supporting evidence myself, I similarly conclude that the hospital report from 2012 does not establish the cause of injuries and the affidavits from the father and neighbour do not indicate the source of their knowledge and do not cure the defects in the Appellant's own testimony. I find that the Appellant faced verbal threats in 2011 due to his support of the SAD(A) party, but that he has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he was physically harmed on three occasions in 2011 and 2012. Role within Shiromani Akali Dal (Amritsar)

In respect of his role within the SAD(A) party, I find that the Appellant was a party member who did work XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, but that he was not an influential or high-profile member of SAD(A). In the March 29, 2020 interview with CBSA, the Appellant stated that he was not a member but supported the SAD(A) party.15 In his BOC form, the Appellant stated that he was a formal member who helped organize political events, campaigned for people to attend the political rallies, and was known as a prominent and active member.16 In testimony before the RPD, the Appellant confirmed that he was responsible for organizing events and would make some comments about DSS when encouraging people to attend SAD(A) rallies,17 but stated that he did not hold a prominent position in SAD(A).18 The letter from SAD(A) confirms the Appellant's permanent membership but does not indicate that he held a position of any prominence.19 The Appellant did not submit additional evidence or make submissions on his role in SAD(A) in this appeal. Conclusion on credibility

I find that the RPD was correct in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility and in its factual determinations that the Appellant was not physically harmed by DSS supporters and was not a high-profile or influential member of SAD(A). I find that the facts surrounding the Appellant's interactions with DSS in the past and his role with SAD(A) are relevant to the issue that is determinative of this appeal, which is whether there is a viable IFA for the Appellant in Delhi. Internal Flight Alternative

The RPD found that there is a viable IFA in Delhi. The RPD correctly identified the two-pronged test for assessing an IFA:20 (1) The Board must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. (2) The conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.

Both prongs of the test must be satisfied to find that a claimant has an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and potential IFAs identified, the burden of proof rests with the claimant to show that he does not have an IFA. First prong of the IFA test

Before the RPD, the Appellant submitted that he would be at risk from DSS supporters throughout India. The RPD found that, based on the previous interactions with DSS supporters, which were limited to verbal threats in 2011, and based on the Appellant's low-level profile and involvement with SAD(A), he has a viable IFA in Delhi. The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD's assessment of his credibility was flawed and that it erroneously concluded that the Appellant had only faced verbal threats in 2011 and not the more severe physical harm the Appellant alleged in his BOC form and RPD hearing. The Appellant did not raise an issue regarding the RPD's finding that he was not a high-profile or influential member of SAD(A).

As explained in the section above, I find the RPD was correct in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility and I conclude, as the RPD did, that the Appellant did not endure the physical harm that he alleged in his BOC form and RPD hearing. I also conclude that the Appellant was not a high-profile or influential member of SAD(A), based on his own description of activities which included helping to organize and promote rallies. I find that the RPD correctly applied these facts in its assessment of the first prong of the IFA test.

I find that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk of torture, risk to his life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Delhi. The Appellant previously spent time in locations within Punjab Province without being located by DSS. The Appellant faced verbal threats and harassment in XXXX XXXX, District Bathinda, Punjab Province in XXXX 2011. Following the incident, the Appellant returned to the Sikh temple (also known as a gurdwara) where he was living in XXXX,21 visited his parents' home in Moga for periods of up to ten days every 2-3 months, and spent 5-6 months in his grandparent's village of XXXX and before leaving for Canada in 2013.22 Although he states that DSS have visited his parents' home and still ask about his whereabouts and threatened to find him, he was never harmed or located while visiting his parents. He states that DSS were not aware of his maternal grandparents' location, so they never located him there.

The DSS did not locate the Appellant in Punjab Province where the DSS operates and where the Appellant has familial connections linking him to specific locations. The Appellant does not have such connections in Delhi, which has a population of over 30 million.23 Evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) on India and from the Appellant indicates that DSS followers are predominately located in Malwa region and have some influence in politics in Punjab and Haryana provinces, but does not indicate that they have a significant presence or influence in Delhi.24

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that he may come to the attention of DSS supporters if he becomes engaged in political activities as he had in 2011. I find that the Appellant has not established that this is likely to occur in Delhi. The Appellant does not indicate that he has engaged in any political activities in the past eight years since coming to Canada. Even if he does decide to engage in political activities or protests in Delhi, the documentary evidence does not support that DSS would be interested or capable of locating the Appellant and harming him. As noted above, the documentary evidence does not indicate that DSS has a strong presence in Delhi. In addition, evidence in the NDP indicates that SAD(A) has held public protests in Delhi as recently as 201925 and actively participates in local, state-level and national parliamentary elections in Punjab and various protests and rallies.26 The evidence does not indicate that SAD(A) members or supporters have been targeted by DSS supporters during these events. Second prong of the IFA test

The Appellant has failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for him to seek refuge in Delhi. On appeal, the Appellant has not raised any issue with the findings of the RPD regarding the second prong of the IFA test. I agree with the RPD that the Appellant could reasonably relocate to Delhi. A review of the most recent NDP for India reveals that Delhi has a Sikh population of 570,581 as of 2011, that Sikhs have access to government assistance programs as a minority community, are economically and socially integrated in communities in which they live and are generally safe.27 The Appellant has worked in various gurdwaras in India and Canada, which have provided him with accommodations, food, and a salary. The Appellant could reasonably access similar employment and practice his religion openly in Delhi. Conclusion on Internal Flight Alternative

Having conducted an independent assessment of the evidence, I conclude that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Delhi. He does not face a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Delhi. It would not be objectively unreasonable in all the circumstances for the Appellant to live in Delhi.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
